kjv: in thy (Isaac's) seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed
mine: by your (Isaac's) offspring all the nations of the earth shall find blessing
note: As in 22:18 the verb is hithpael (hitbarakhu), most naturally reflexive ("bless themselves by", i.e. invoke as a model of blessing); the KJV takes it as passive with the LXX. Context: find blessing (keeps passive and reflexive senses open) (low confidence). The hithpael hitbarakhu (as 22:18) is normally reflexive, 'bless themselves' (cf. 48:20), but the parallel promises use the niphal (12:3; 18:18; 28:14), the hithpael can carry middle/passive force, and LXX, Vulgate and the NT (Acts 3:25; Gal 3:8) read 'be blessed'. The evidence is balanced; 'find blessing' keeps both senses. Other possible meanings: (1) 'shall be blessed' (receive blessing through the offspring) — LXX eneulogethesontai, Vulgate benedicentur, Acts 3:25, Gal 3:8, KJV, ESV, NIV, NASB, CSB; (2) 'shall bless themselves by' (invoke the offspring as a model of blessing, cf. 48:20) — NJPS, NET ('pronounce blessings ... using the name'), NRSV ('gain blessing for themselves'), many critical commentators.
Hebrew metsaheq (the Isaac wordplay again) here denotes conjugal fondling that showed she was his wife; "sporting" now suggests merely playing.

kjv: might lightly have lien with thy (Isaac's) wife
mine: might easily have lain with your (Isaac's) wife
note: Hebrew kim'at, "almost, easily"; KJV "lightly" meant easily, but a modern reader may take it as "casually".
Hebrew merea, "companion, friend", appears to be a court title ("the king's friend", cf. 2 Sam 15:37); the KJV "one of his friends" also needlessly adds "one of".
